notes.meaning: King Xerxes placed a tax or forced labor across his vast empire, extending all the way to the distant coasts and islands. After the crisis caused by Haman was settled, ordinary government work resumed, and the king needed to refill the imperial treasury. This shows that God's quiet care for His people carries on through the ordinary affairs of civil life.

The writer directs the reader to the official royal records of Media and Persia for a fuller account of the king's power and Mordecai's high rank. Mordecai's wise work helped the whole kingdom prosper, earning him a lasting name in the court records of a pagan nation. Those Persian archives were eventually lost, but God preserved the biblical record to encourage His people in every generation.

Mordecai was appointed second in command over the entire empire, serving as the king's prime minister. He never used his high office for selfish gain or forgot his heritage, but worked faithfully for the protection and well-being of his fellow Jews. His rise from sitting in rags at the palace gate to ruling near the throne demonstrates how God honors humble, upright servants to bless others.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, the chapter does not end at verse 3. It continues with ten more verses and several additional chapters from the ancient Greek translation, in which Mordecai explains a prophetic dream and openly gives thanks to God.
